name: Zoe Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the shepherd's assistant at Highfold, a hill estate with about fourteen hundred ewes on open hill, rough grazing that goes up past the tree line. In winter it's feeding the ewes on the lower ground, checking for any that are stuck or lame, and walking. So much walking. Morag, the head shepherd, does the thinking, and I carry the feed bags and try to get my dog to listen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up on a hill farm at your age?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a care assistant for twenty years at a care home in the city, lifting and washing and feeding people. My back went, and when my partner Dev got a job driving the gritting lorries out here, I saw the Highfold advert pinned up at the shop. Morag said she'd take anyone who could stand the weather, and I said I'd stood worse than weather.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the gather in September, when the dogs bring the whole hill down and you see the flock pour off the slope like water. What wears me out is my own dog, Meg. She's two, she's keen, and she listens to Morag better than she listens to me, which is humbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, that's nice for the people in offices. Up here it's weather, grass and sheep, and none of those read the news. I might mention it in the WhatsApp group with my old care home friends, because they do all their notes on tablets now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I already use it now and then. I asked one of those chat things how to teach a dog to lie down at a distance, and it was about half right. Morag laughed and said the other half is called patience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep saving what I can, which is about three months' worth at the moment, finish paying off Dev's van. Maybe do the sheep scanning course in the spring, if the estate pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a tool, like a better torch for lambing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your old care home friends say about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joy would say it's helped with the paperwork, which used to eat an hour of every shift. Joy's sensible. If it means more time sitting with Mrs Price and less time typing, I'm all for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a better torch for lambing. What's lambing like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's April, three weeks of hardly sleeping, sheds full of ewes and the ones on the hill giving birth wherever they please. Last year I pulled my first lamb on my own, a big tup lamb stuck with one leg back. I cried after, in the quad bike, where nobody could see.

S0.say: I'd say it's nice for people in offices, but up here it's weather, grass and sheep. I'd maybe mention it to my old care home friends who use tablets now.
S0.think: I already use it now and then, like asking how to train a dog to lie down at a distance. It was about half right, and the other half is patience.
S0.do: Keeps saving and finishes paying off Dev's van. Considers the sheep scanning course in spring if the estate pays for it.
S0.feel: Calm, as if someone had made a better lambing torch.
S0.quote: I asked one of those chat things how to teach a dog to lie down at a distance, and it was about half right.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe talks about the hill with real love, and about her own skill with plain modesty. She already uses AI casually and without fuss. Her old life in the care home is still very present; she checks in with those friends first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say hill farming stopped hiring beginners years ago, so welcome to our world. Highfold used to have three shepherds and now it's Morag and me. I'd say we need public money for training, the same way we got grants for walls and hedges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm lucky Morag took a chance on an old beginner. If everyone hires fewer beginners, there won't be a next one after me, and Morag retires in four years. I worry the estate would just let the hill go wild rather than train someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Morag to teach me everything she knows faster, the hill routes, the ewes' habits, which ones always go to the same corner. I'd write it down in a notebook. And I'd put the scanning course on my list for sure, not maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but more for the hill than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's in that notebook so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much yet, and the handwriting is bad because I write in the cold. There's a page about the north face, where the ewes shelter by a broken wall in a storm. Morag's known that for thirty years and it's in no book anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's the next beginner, if there is one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a girl at the village school, Ffion, who comes up at lambing to bottle-feed the orphans. She's fifteen and she's brilliant with the dogs. If the jobs aren't there for her, she'll go to the city like everyone else.

S1.say: I'd say hill farming stopped hiring beginners years ago, so welcome to our world. We need public money for training, like the grants for walls and hedges.
S1.think: I think I was lucky Morag took a chance on an old beginner, and there may not be another after me. I worry the estate would let the hill go wild instead of training someone.
S1.do: Asks Morag to teach her the hill faster and starts a notebook of routes and ewe habits. Signs up for the scanning course instead of just thinking about it.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, more for the hill and its knowledge than for herself.
S1.quote: Morag's known that for thirty years and it's in no book anywhere.
S1.fieldNote: She immediately framed fewer beginners as a threat to knowledge, not to her pay. The notebook says a lot: she's steady, not panicked, but she wants to catch what Morag knows before it walks off the hill. She has a named hope for the future, a fifteen-year-old called Ffion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office workers need a union, fast, and the government should protect pay while this settles. I'd share the petitions, I always do. And I'd say farming still needs people, come up the hill if you want a job that's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be thinking about my daughter. Sana's an accounts clerk at a builders' firm, invoices and payroll, and that's routine office work if anything is. She's got a mortgage and a little boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring Sana that week and ask her straight what her firm is doing with these AI things. I'd keep my own savings where they are, because if she needs help with the mortgage, it comes from us. And I'd try one of those AI helpers properly, so I understand what she's up against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like watching weather coming in over the top of the hill toward someone else's house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said come up the hill if you want a real job. Would you say that to Sana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's a bit rich of me, isn't it. Sana hates mud and she'd last a day. I'd say it to strangers on the internet, not to my own daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Sana needed money, what would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday Dev and I were going to have, a week at the coast in June. We've not had one in four years. It'd go first, and I'd pretend I didn't mind.

S2.say: I'd say office workers need a union and the government should protect pay while this settles. I'd share the petitions and tell people farming still needs hands.
S2.think: Privately I'd be thinking about my daughter Sana, an accounts clerk with a mortgage and a little boy. Invoices and payroll are routine office work if anything is.
S2.do: Rings Sana that week to ask what her firm is doing with AI and keeps savings ready to help with the mortgage. Tries an AI helper properly to understand what Sana faces.
S2.feel: Uneasy, like watching bad weather move toward someone else's house.
S2.quote: I'd say it to strangers on the internet, not to my own daughter.
S2.fieldNote: She caught her own contradiction before I finished asking it, and laughed at herself. Her public line is the classic progressive one, unions and protection, but her private worry is entirely about Sana. She'd give up the first holiday in four years without a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fourth one is faster. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should go to people who do the work, not to whoever already owns the most. I'd go to a protest if there was one in town. Online I'd be sharing things about a tax on the big winners, and arguing with my cousin about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the boom worries me for the hill. When rich people have money to spare, they buy hill estates to plant trees and sell carbon credits, payments for soaking up pollution. If Highfold's owner gets an offer like that, the sheep go and so do I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Morag what she's heard about the owner's plans, because she hears things at the auction mart. I'd look at the other hill farms nearby, there are a few, and find out who's hiring. And I'd push Sana to keep her mortgage payments going whatever it takes, even if we help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not robots that would take my job in this one. It's someone's spare money looking for somewhere to sit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has that happened near you before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two valleys over, Coldside was sold three years ago and planted with spruce. The shepherd there, Huw, moved to a dairy farm in the lowlands and he says he misses the hill every day. The place is just rows of little trees and a locked gate now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Sana's job is at risk here. What would you tell her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her she's got a good head and she'll find something, and I'd believe it for maybe half of the conversation. Then I'd go out to the dogs and worry properly. Sheepdogs are good listeners, better than Dev.

S3.say: I'd say the gains should go to people who do the work, not to whoever already owns the most. I'd protest in town and share posts about taxing the big winners.
S3.think: I worry the boom means rich buyers turn the hill into tree plantations for carbon credits. If Highfold's owner gets that offer, the sheep go and so do I.
S3.do: Asks Morag what she's heard at the auction mart about the owner's plans and checks which nearby hill farms are hiring. Urges Sana to keep her mortgage payments going, with help if needed.
S3.feel: Anxious, because the threat comes from spare money looking for a home rather than from machines.
S3.quote: It's not robots that would take my job in this one. It's someone's spare money looking for somewhere to sit.
S3.fieldNote: Like several hill workers, she sees land deals as a bigger threat than technology. She has a real example in Coldside, two valleys over. She reassures her daughter out loud and then worries in private with the dogs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This is the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots should work for us, not instead of us, and every farm that buys one should be paying into training for the people it replaces. And I'd say it about the care homes even louder. My old residents deserve a human hand, not a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the hill buys me some time, I think. It's steep, wet and rocky, and nothing with wheels gets up the north face. But they're already trying collars on the ewes that keep them in with a beep instead of a fence, and drones for counting. A robot can't climb the crag in sleet and read a ewe's face. But I said that about the collars, and now half the flock wears one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever runs the collars and the drones, once I've seen it work on someone else's hill first. I'd ask the estate to send me on the course, and if they won't, I'd pay half myself. And I'd keep a bit more in savings, aim for five months instead of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not panicked. I've seen the hill beat clever things before. But I think about Mrs Price in the care home being fed by a machine, and that's the part that makes me want to cry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the collars.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estate trialled them on two hundred ewes last year. The sheep learn the beep and turn back, and Morag can move the invisible fence from her phone. I hated it at first, now I check the map on the app most mornings, so there you go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most, at Highfold or back at the care home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The care home, honestly. Joy's fifty-four and she's on her feet twelve hours a day for not much money. If the robots come in there, she's got nothing else to go to, and the residents get something that can lift them but can't hold their hand.

S4.say: I'd say robots should work for us, not instead of us, and farms that buy them should pay for training. I'd say it even louder about the care homes.
S4.think: I think the steep, wet hill buys me some time because nothing with wheels gets up the north face. But I said that about the collars, and now half the flock wears one.
S4.do: Learns the collar and drone systems once she's seen them work elsewhere, asks the estate to pay for training and would pay half herself if needed. Aims to build savings from three months to five.
S4.feel: Anxious, not panicked, but close to tears thinking of old care home residents being fed by a machine.
S4.quote: A robot can't climb the crag in sleet and read a ewe's face. But I said that about the collars, and now half the flock wears one.
S4.fieldNote: Zoe argued with herself in real time: the hill protects her, and then the collars prove it doesn't. She's already using the new tech she first resisted, which fits her steady pattern. The strongest feeling came not about sheep but about care home residents and her friend Joy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, but mostly because of the care homes, not because of me. What would help is public money to train people like me on the new kit, and a law that a person, not a machine, has to be there when someone's being cared for. For the hill, I'd want support payments tied to keeping people working the land, not just trees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dogs. If robots do the gathering, nobody breeds a good working dog anymore, and that's a hundred years of knowledge gone in one generation. Meg's not good yet, but she's trying, same as me.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Thank you. Now I have to go and find out why Meg's barking at the feed bin.

headlineQuote: A robot can't climb the crag in sleet and read a ewe's face. But I said that about the collars, and now half the flock wears one.
portrait: Zoe is a 58-year-old shepherd's assistant on a hill sheep estate, a former care assistant who came to farming three years ago and is still learning to handle her young dog. She leans progressive, wants public money for training and support, and uses AI tools now and then. Her worries move from her daughter's office job, to rich buyers planting trees over the hill, to robots in care homes where her old friends still work. She resists new kit at first, then uses it once it has proved itself.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries her most, more because of care homes and her friend Joy than because of her own job on the hill.
whatWouldHelp: Public money to train people like her on new equipment, a law that a person must be present in care, and hill support payments tied to keeping people working the land.
